children: Source of authority – people of India
Nature of Indian State – sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republican
Objectives of the Constitution – justice, liberty, equality, fraternity
Date of adoption – November 26, 1949
India is neither a dependency nor a dominion of any other nation
Independent state; no authority above India
Freedom to conduct own affairs (internal and external)
Commonwealth membership does not affect sovereignty
UNO membership does not limit sovereignty
Power to acquire foreign territory
Power to cede territory in favour of a foreign state
India ceased to be a British dominion on January 26, 1950
India declared herself a sovereign republic on January 26, 1950
Implicit socialist content in Directive Principles made explicit by 42nd Amendment
Congress party resolution for 'socialistic pattern of society' (Avadi session 1955)
Democratic socialism (mixed economy, public and private sectors co-exist)
Supreme Court defined democratic socialism as ending poverty, ignorance, disease and inequality
Indian socialism as a blend of Marxism and Gandhism
New Economic Policy (1991) – liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation diluted socialist credentials
Principal means of production under social ownership, equitable distribution of national wealth
Supreme Court (1974): secular state intended by Constitution-makers

Positive concept of secularism: all religions have same status and support from state
State is neutral, does not uphold any particular religion
State treats every religion equally
State does not have any foundation of religion
India is a secular state (along with USA)

concepts.text: Types of states based on attitude towards religion
children: Atheistic State – state is anti-religion, condemns all religions
Theocratic State – state is pro-religion, declares one religion as state religion (examples: Bangladesh, Burma, Sri Lanka, Pakistan)
Secular State – state neutral, does not uphold any religion (examples: USA, India)
Term democracy derived from Greek Demos (people) and Kratia (rule)
Doctrine of popular sovereignty
Direct democracy methods: Referendum, Initiative, Recall, Plebiscite
Indirect/Representative democracy: representatives elected by people
Parliamentary democracy: executive responsible to legislature
Universal adult franchise
Periodic elections
Rule of law
Independence of judiciary
Political democracy
Social democracy
Economic democracy
Dr. Ambedkar: social democracy as a way of life recognising liberty, equality and fraternity
Head of state elected indirectly for fixed period of five years (President of India)
Vesting of political sovereignty in the people
Absence of any privileged class
All public offices open to every citizen without discrimination
Social justice: equal treatment without social distinction, improvement of backward classes and women
Economic justice: non-discrimination, elimination of inequalities, distributive justice
Political justice: equal political rights, access to offices, voice in government
Ideal of justice taken from Russian Revolution (1917)
Absence of restraints on activities of individuals
Providing opportunities for development of individual personalities
Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship secured through Fundamental Rights
Liberty is not absolute but qualified, enjoyed within limitations mentioned in the Constitution
Liberty does not mean license to do what one likes
Ideals of liberty taken from French Revolution (1789-1799)
Absence of special privileges to any section of society
Provision of adequate opportunities for all individuals without discrimination
Three dimensions: civic, political, economic
Constitutional provisions: Articles 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 325, 326, 39
Ideals of equality taken from French Revolution
Sense of brotherhood
Single citizenship
Fundamental Duties (Article 51-A): promote harmony and common brotherhood
Dignity of the individual
Unity and integrity of the nation (Integrity added by 42nd Amendment)

Article 1: India as 'Union of States' – states cannot secede
Hindrances to national integration: communalism, regionalism, casteism, linguism, secessionism

concepts.text: Interrelationship of Liberty, Equality and Fraternity (as per Dr. Ambedkar)
children: Liberty, equality and fraternity as a union of trinity
Liberty cannot be divorced from equality
Equality cannot be divorced from liberty
Liberty and equality cannot be divorced from fraternity
Without equality, liberty produces supremacy of the few over the many
Equality without liberty kills individual initiative
Berubari Union case (1960): Preamble is not a part of the Constitution
Kesavananda Bharati case (1973): Preamble is a part of the Constitution
LIC of India case (1995): Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution
Preamble is non-justiciable (not enforceable in courts)
Preamble is neither a source of power nor a prohibition upon legislature
Preamble can be amended under Article 368 but cannot alter the basic features
Basic elements enshrined in the Preamble cannot be destroyed (sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republic, justice, liberty, equality, fraternity)
Preamble amended only once (1976) by 42nd Amendment – added Socialist, Secular and Integrity
President of the Constituent Assembly stated the Preamble stands part of the Constitution
Moved by Pandit Nehru on December 13, 1946
